description_full: Ferrari N.V., through its subsidiaries, engages in design, engineering, production, and sale of luxury performance sports cars worldwide. It offers sports, track, one-off, and road cars, as well as supercars. The company also provides spare parts and engines, as well as after sales, repair, maintenance, and restoration services for cars; and licenses its Ferrari brand to various producers and retailers of luxury and lifestyle goods. In addition, it operates Ferrari museums in Modena and Maranello; Il Cavallino restaurant in Maranello; and theme parks in Abu Dhabi and Spain. Further, the company provides direct or indirect finance and leasing services; range of financial and ancillary services; special financing arrangements; and operates franchised and owned Ferrari stores. The company was founded in 1947 and is headquartered in Maranello, Italy.

financial_summary: Ferrari N.V. is a large-cap consumer cyclical business with a $72.0B market cap on $7.9B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +15% over the past three years, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.
Returns on capital run at 31% against a 9% cost of capital — a 22-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat.

The business throws off $2.1B in free cash flow — roughly 26 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.47× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.5× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 9.8×.

Shareholder yield is only 0.8%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 32% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and within its sector the business captures 3.7× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.
